the measurement and control of emissions of hazardous air pollutants, particularly mutagenic emissions, from the incinerator combustion of hazardous organic wastes.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the staged combustion process is the preferred NO x control technology, because it is more effective in reducing NO x emissions and does not increase the mutagenic emissions.

the use of staged combustion and/or reburning technologies for the control of NO x from a burner/package boiler system burning dinoseb as the sole fuel source resulted in a significant decrease in the mutagenicity and toxicity of the particle-bound organic fraction and the semivolatile dicholoromethane-extracted organics of the flue gases.

the staged-combustion and reburning technologies, as applied in this study, did not significantly reduce the mutagenicity or toxicity of the incineration emissions from the pesticide dinoseb, and that the combustion-modification technologies, as applied, did not significantly alter the mutagenic or toxicity profile of the emissions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the combustion-modification technologies employed in this study were effective in reducing the mutagenic emissions.
the staged combustion process was effective for NO x control but was not as effective for reducing the mutagenicity in the particle-bound and extractable organics.
the combustion modifications were effective in controlling the mutagenicity in both the particle and semivolatile fractions of the emissions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
combustion modifications can significantly reduce the mutagenicity and toxicity of emissions from the incinera tion of the pesticide dinoseb.

the Ames assay is a useful tool for evaluating the mutagenic emissions of a combustion process and can be used to monitor the effectiveness of combustion modifications for controlling mutagenic emissions.
